Consult Summary:
- 35-year-old man (lawyer) with new-onset, work-associated frontal headaches, intermittent palpitations and shortness of breath at rest, bilateral hand tingling, decreased appetite with ~5 lb unintentional weight loss, and reduced libido since a recent job change; history of thyroid disease on thyroxine. Plan: in-person evaluation with cardiorespiratory exam and thyroid-related blood tests.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Headaches, intermittent palpitations (heart beating fast), intermittent shortness of breath at rest, bilateral hand tingling, decreased appetite, reduced libido.
- Timeline:
  - Symptoms began around the time he changed jobs.
  - Headaches occur mostly at work (in meetings or on laptop), front of head, non-radiating.
  - Palpitations occur approximately daily (sometimes more), noted especially in the elevator in the morning.
  - Shortness of breath occurs while sitting at his desk; not with exercise.
  - Reduced appetite with unintentional ~5 lb weight loss; libido decreased over the same period.
- Associated symptoms:
  - Headache sometimes associated with mild nausea.
  - Tingling described as “quick picking” in both hands; no leg involvement.
- Exacerbating/relieving factors:
  - Headaches occur during work-related activities (laptop, meetings).
  - Palpitations noted in elevator; shortness of breath at rest (desk).
  - No shortness of breath with exercise.
- Pertinent negatives/other:
  - No prior history of headaches before this period.
  - Headaches not typically on the commute.
  - Patient reported symptoms generally happen one at a time, not all together.
  - Initial triage note stated “feeling hot,” but patient later described shortness of breath instead (conflict noted).

Past Medical History:
- Thyroid disease:
  - Patient reports “hyperthyroidism.”
  - Medication: taking thyroxine (see Medications). Conflict noted between diagnosis and medication type.
  - Adherence: reports taking medication as prescribed.

Medications:
- Thyroxine — dose/route/frequency not documented; patient reports good adherence.

Allergies:
- Not documented.

Social History:
- Occupation: Lawyer in London; approximately 50% meetings and 50% computer work; high reading load.
- Work-related stress: 7–8/10; typical for law firm per patient.
- Alcohol: ~once per week, a couple of glasses of wine.
- Tobacco: Denies smoking.
- Recreational drugs: Denies; specifically denies cocaine and marijuana.
- Sexual: Reports reduced libido since job change.

Family History:
- Not mentioned.

Physical Examination:
- Not performed (telehealth). No vitals documented.

Investigations:
- None completed during this encounter.
- Planned: Blood tests “for your thyroxine” (thyroid-related labs; specific tests not documented).

Assessment & Plan:
- Issue 1: Recurrent frontal headaches, work-associated, occasional nausea, new since job change.
  - Plan: In-person clinic visit; defer medications until examined.
- Issue 2: Intermittent palpitations and shortness of breath at rest (not with exercise), approximately daily.
  - Plan: In-person assessment with heart and breathing examination.
- Issue 3: Bilateral hand tingling (“quick picking”), new onset.
  - Plan: Evaluate in clinic during in-person visit.
- Issue 4: Decreased appetite, ~5 lb unintentional weight loss; reduced libido.
  - Plan: Assess in clinic; proceed with planned thyroid-related blood tests.
- Issue 5: Thyroid disease on thyroxine (diagnosis–medication mismatch).
  - Plan: Perform thyroid-related blood tests; clarify thyroid diagnosis and reconcile medication at in-person visit.
- General plan:
  - Book in-person appointment via app.
  - No new medications before in-person evaluation.
  - Clinician will brief colleague prior to visit.

Quality checks:
- Missing expected elements: Vitals, physical exam, detailed headache characterization (duration per episode, severity scale, photophobia/phonophobia), red flag screening (fever, neck stiffness, focal deficits, vision changes), cardiovascular ROS (chest pain, syncope), sleep, mood/anxiety screen, full medication list with doses, allergies confirmation, family history.
- Internal conflicts:
  - Initial note of “feeling hot” vs patient later emphasizing shortness of breath at rest.
  - Patient-reported “hyperthyroidism” while taking thyroxine (typically for hypothyroidism).
  - Allergy status unclear; clinician responded “Good,” but no explicit patient statement captured.
- Transcript quality: Some fragmented/inaudible portions and hesitations; adequate to extract key clinical details but several specifics (timing, severity, allergy status) remain unclear.
